newsitem.title: UK: British inflation edges up, government to amend target.
newsitem.headline: British inflation edges up, government to amend target.

text.p: Britain's headline annual inflation rate edged higher in May and price rises were once again particularly strong in the service sector, which accounts for two-thirds of the economy.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Thursday that the retail price index rose 0.4 percent in May from the previous month, giving an annual inflation rate of 2.6 percent compared with 2.4 percent in April.
Underlying inflation, the measure targeted by the government which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, was unchanged at 2.5 percent.

But economists said inflation in the service sector of the economy, which was unchanged at 3.3 percent for the fourth month in a row, was worryingly strong. This compared with goods price inflation of just 1.7 percent. "We've got strong growth in services bringing a strong threat of inflation," said David Bloom, economist at HSBC James Capel.
James Capel's own measure of service inflation, stripping out utilities prices which fell one percent in the year to May, shows prices rising at 3.9 percent a year.
Other economists said the inflation outlook remained benign.
"This morning's data were rather encouraging as prices showed subdued pressures in most sectors of the economy," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, an economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"These data, combined with some good producer price numbers earlier this week, should take some pressure off the Bank of England to continue its monetary tightening."
Prices leaving the factory gate rose just one percent in the year to May.
New Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown was expected to make some amendments to the inflation target in a major speech at London's Mansion House on Thursday evening.

Newspapers reported that in his set-piece address to the City, Brown would stick to the 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation which he inherited from the Conservatives, but drop the words "or less."

This means that the Bank of England, newly empowered by Brown to set interest rates to meet the target, would have to try to avoid undershooting 2.5 percent -- thereby deflating the economy -- as well as overshooting it.
The Financial Times and two other newspapers said Brown would impose penalties on the Bank if it missed the 2.5 percent target by one percent on either side.

"If this is correct, the new target will be slightly easier to hit than the old one," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers. "Effectively the Chancellor is aiming for a slightly looser target."
Ian Stewart of Merrill Lynch said the newspaper reports pointed to a softening in monetary policy.
"The current target, effectively a band between zero and 2.5 percent, is being replaced by a higher band of 1.5 to 3.5 percent," he said.

The Bank of England, which has been sounding warnings about inflation since the end of last year, made use of its new powers for the first time last week, raising official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent.

The ONS said the pickup in overall inflation in May was due mainly to housing costs. There was a small upward effect from higher prices for alcoholic drinks while motoring costs and household goods prices eased.
